description: A devastating disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It produces dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems.
steps: Remove and destroy all infected plant parts immediately
Apply copper-based fungicide (Bordeaux mixture) as soon as symptoms appear
Spray chlorothalonil or mancozeb every 7-10 days during wet weather
Improve air circulation by proper plant spacing
Avoid overhead watering — use drip irrigation instead
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Rotate crops — avoid planting tomatoes in the same spot for 3 years
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash
Plant resistant varieties such as 'Mountain Magic' or 'Defiant'
organicAlternatives: Baking soda solution (1 tbsp per gallon of water)

description: Caused by Alternaria solani, this disease creates concentric ring patterns (target spots) on lower leaves first.
steps: Remove infected lower leaves and destroy them
Apply fungicide containing chlorothalonil or copper
Spray at 7-14 day intervals during growing season
Stake or cage plants to keep foliage off the ground
prevention: Rotate crops on a 2-3 year cycle
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering
Maintain adequate plant nutrition, especially potassium

description: Caused by Xanthomonas bacteria, it creates small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit.
steps: Remove and destroy severely infected plants
Apply copper-based bactericide
Avoid overhead irrigation
Disinfect pruning tools between plants
prevention: Avoid working in the field when plants are wet
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
organicAlternatives: Plant-based elicitors to boost plant immunity

description: The same pathogen as tomato late blight (P. infestans). It causes rapid destruction of foliage and tuber rot.
steps: Apply systemic fungicides such as metalaxyl or dimethomorph
Destroy all infected plant material by burning
Hill up soil around potato plants to protect tubers
Harvest early if infection is severe
prevention: Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles
Monitor weather conditions for blight-favorable periods

description: Caused by Alternaria solani, producing dark concentric ring lesions on leaves, starting from the bottom of the plant.
steps: Apply protectant fungicides at first sign of disease
Remove and destroy infected foliage
Maintain adequate fertilization to support plant vigor
Ensure proper plant spacing for airflow

description: Caused by Exserohilum turcicum, it produces long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan lesions on corn leaves.
steps: Apply foliar fungicides containing azoxystrobin or propiconazole
Time applications at first sign of disease, typically at tasseling
Scout fields regularly for early detection
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids with Ht genes
Tillage to bury infected crop residue

description: Caused by Puccinia sorghi, it produces small, round to elongate, cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
steps: Apply fungicide if more than 50% of leaves are affected before tasseling
Use triazole or strobilurin fungicides
Monitor disease progression weekly
prevention: Early planting to avoid late-season rust buildup
Scout fields regularly starting at V8 growth stage
organicAlternatives: Balanced soil nutrition to boost plant immunity

description: Caused by Guignardia bidwellii, it causes tan leaf spots and shriveled, black mummified fruit.
steps: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil or captan) at bud break
Continue applications through bloom and berry development
Remove and destroy mummified fruit and infected canes
Prune vines for good air circulation
prevention: Sanitation — remove all mummies from vines and ground
Choose resistant grape varieties when possible

description: Caused by Venturia inaequalis, it produces olive-green to dark brown velvety lesions on leaves and fruit.
steps: Apply fungicide (captan, myclobutanil) at green-tip stage
Continue protective sprays through petal fall
Remove fallen infected leaves in autumn
Prune for open canopy and air movement
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties (Liberty, Enterprise, Pristine)
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Apply urea to fallen leaves to speed decomposition

description: Caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae, it creates bright yellow-orange spots on apple leaves and fruit.
steps: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil or triadimefon) at pink bud stage
Continue applications through bloom
Remove nearby cedar/juniper trees if possible (alternate host)
prevention: Remove cedar/juniper trees within 1-2 miles if feasible
Monitor for cedar galls in spring and remove them
organicAlternatives: Proper sanitation of alternate host plants

description: Caused by Diplocarpon earlianum, it produces irregular purplish spots that enlarge and cause leaves to dry up.
steps: Remove and destroy infected leaves
Apply fungicides containing captan or thiram
Avoid overhead watering
Renovate strawberry beds after harvest
prevention: Provide adequate spacing for air circulation

description: Caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria, producing small, dark, raised spots on leaves and fruit.
steps: Apply copper-based bactericide mixed with mancozeb
Remove severely infected plants
Avoid overhead irrigation
Use drip watering systems
prevention: Hot water seed treatment (125°F for 25 minutes)
organicAlternatives: Foliar calcium applications to strengthen cell walls

description: Caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, it produces diamond-shaped lesions on leaves and can destroy entire panicles.
steps: Apply systemic fungicides (tricyclazole, isoprothiolane) at first sign
Drain excess water from fields during active infection
Split nitrogen applications to avoid excess growth
Remove infected plant debris after harvest
organicAlternatives: Silicon amendments to strengthen plant cells

description: Caused by Puccinia species, producing orange-brown (leaf rust) or dark brown (stem rust) pustules on wheat leaves and stems.
steps: Apply foliar fungicides (propiconazole, tebuconazole) at first sign
Scout fields regularly during heading and grain fill stages
Consider aerial application for large fields
prevention: Early planting to avoid peak rust season
Eliminate volunteer wheat and alternate hosts

description: No disease detected. The plant appears healthy with no visible symptoms of infection.
steps: Continue regular monitoring and maintenance
Maintain optimal watering schedule
Apply balanced fertilization as needed
Keep area weed-free
prevention: Regular crop scouting (weekly during growing season)
Ensure proper drainage and air circulation
organicAlternatives: Companion planting for natural pest control
